title: Reading and Writing Files
summary: Python can read text from a file and write text into a file. The file can keep information after the program ends.
introduction: Python can read text from a file and write text into a file. The file can keep information after the program ends. Try this with a new practice file. Learn which mode reads, which adds more text and which replaces old text.
learningObjectives: Read and write text files with open() inside a with statement
Choose between the r, w, a and x modes and always specify an encoding
Process a file line by line without loading all of it into memory
Work with paths, folders and CSV files using pathlib and csv

blocks.title: write.py
blocks.code:
with open("notes.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("Buy milk\n")
    file.write("Call Grace\n")
    file.writelines(["Fix the bike\n", "Read a chapter\n"])

print("Saved notes.txt")

blocks.text: `open()` returns a file object. `"w"` means write, creating the file or emptying an existing one, and `encoding="utf-8"` makes the file readable on every operating system; in Python 3.13 the default encoding still depends on the platform (Windows often uses a legacy code page), so always state it; Python 3.15 finally makes UTF-8 the default, but stating it costs nothing and works everywhere. The `with` statement guarantees that the file is closed when the block ends, even if an exception is raised inside it; without it, text can sit in a buffer and never reach the disk. `write()` does not add line breaks, so you include `\n` yourself.

blocks.title: read.py
blocks.code:
with open("notes.txt", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    content = file.read()
print(repr(content))
print(len(content.splitlines()), "lines")

with open("notes.txt", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    for number, line in enumerate(file, start=1):
        print(f"{number}: {line.rstrip()}")

with open("notes.txt", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    lines = file.readlines()
print(lines[0].strip(), "|", lines[-1].strip())

blocks.title: python read.py
blocks.content:
'Buy milk\nCall Grace\nFix the bike\nRead a chapter\n'
4 lines
1: Buy milk
2: Call Grace
3: Fix the bike
4: Read a chapter
Buy milk | Read a chapter

blocks.text: Mode `"r"` (read) is the default. `read()` returns the whole file as one string, which is fine for small files. Looping over the file object yields one line at a time, including its trailing `\n` (hence the `rstrip()`), and never holds more than one line in memory, so it works for files of any size. `readlines()` gives a list of lines for when you need indexing. The file position moves as you read, which is why each example reopens the file.

rows: Read (the default); `FileNotFoundError` if the file is missing
Write; creates the file or empties an existing one
Append at the end; creates the file if missing
Create a new file; `FileExistsError` if it already exists
Binary read or write (images, archives): `bytes` instead of `str`, no encoding
Read and write the same file

blocks.title: "w" erases the file immediately
blocks.text: Opening an existing file with `"w"` empties it the moment `open()` returns, before you write anything, and there is no undo. To add to a file use `"a"`; to refuse to overwrite use `"x"`. When a script must rewrite a file it also reads, read everything first, close the file, then open it again for writing.

blocks.title: append.py
blocks.code:
with open("notes.txt", "a", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("Water the plants\n")

with open("notes.txt", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    print(file.read().count("\n"), "lines now")

try:
    with open("missing.txt", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        print(file.read())
except FileNotFoundError as error:
    print("Error:", error)

blocks.title: python append.py
blocks.content:
5 lines now
Error: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'missing.txt'

blocks.text: Opening a file that does not exist for reading raises `FileNotFoundError`, one of the most common exceptions in real programs; catch it where you can do something useful, such as creating a default configuration, and let it propagate otherwise (see [Errors and Exceptions](/tutorials/python/errors-exceptions)).

blocks.title: paths.py
blocks.code:
from pathlib import Path

folder = Path("archive")
folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

target = folder / "2026-11-15.txt"
target.write_text("First entry\n", encoding="utf-8")
print(target.name, target.exists(), target.suffix)
print(target.read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip())
print(target.stem, target.parent.name)

(folder / "2026-11-16.txt").write_text("Second entry\n", encoding="utf-8")
print(sorted(p.name for p in folder.glob("*.txt")))

blocks.text: `pathlib.Path` represents a path as an object. The `/` operator joins parts with the right separator for the operating system (a backslash on Windows, a slash elsewhere), `mkdir`, `exists`, `glob`, `read_text` and `write_text` cover the daily file operations, and `.name`, `.stem`, `.suffix` and `.parent` take a path apart without string surgery. `Path.home()` and `Path.cwd()` give the home folder and the current working directory. Prefer `pathlib` over the older `os.path` functions in new code.

Spreadsheets and databases export comma-separated values. The `csv` module handles quoting and commas inside values, which a naive `split(",")` gets wrong, and its `DictWriter` and `DictReader` map each row to a dictionary keyed by the header line.

blocks.title: scores.py
blocks.code:
import csv
from pathlib import Path

rows = [
    {"name": "Mina", "city": "Lisbon", "score": 82},
    {"name": "Ravi", "city": "Nairobi", "score": 91},
]
with open("scores.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(file, fieldnames=["name", "city", "score"])
    writer.writeheader()
    writer.writerows(rows)

with open("scores.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    for row in csv.DictReader(file):
        print(row["name"], int(row["score"]) + 5)

print(Path("scores.csv").read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip())

blocks.text: Pass `newline=""` when opening CSV files, as the documentation requires; otherwise Windows gets a blank line between rows. Every value read from a CSV file is a string, so convert numbers yourself, as `int(row["score"])` does. For large or complex tables, [pandas](/tutorials/pandas) reads a CSV file into a typed table with a single call.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Write a script that appends one line with the current date to `journal.txt` every time it runs (`from datetime import date` and `date.today()`), then prints how many entries the journal has.

questions.question: `with open(...) as file:` closes the file automatically when the block ends, even if an exception is raised inside it.
questions.explanation: That is the whole point of the `with` statement: the file object's clean-up runs on every exit from the block, normal or not.

questions.question: Which mode adds text at the end of an existing file without deleting its current content?
questions.explanation: `"a"` appends. `"w"` truncates the file first, `"x"` refuses to open an existing file, and `"r+"` starts writing at the beginning, overwriting what is there.
